blurb: How qubits really work, what quantum computers can and can't do, and why error correction decides everything.

cards.title: Bits, qubits and interference

steps.p: A normal bit is 0 or 1. Every app, photo and website is ultimately billions of these tiny switches.
A qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1, described by two amplitudes. Measuring it forces a definite 0 or 1.
Algorithms arrange amplitudes so wrong answers cancel and right answers reinforce, like waves. That only works for problems with special structure.

cards.aside: The popular line that a quantum computer "tries every answer at once" is wrong — you only ever read out one result.

cards.q: You measure a qubit that is in superposition. What do you get?
options: A single 0 or 1, with odds set by its amplitudes
cards.why: One definite bit. Measurement returns 0 or 1 at random, with probabilities from the squared amplitudes. You can't read out the whole superposition, which is why algorithms need clever interference.

cards.statement: A quantum computer speeds up any problem by trying all possible answers in parallel.
cards.why: False. Measurement gives only one outcome. Speedups come from interference that boosts correct answers, which works only for problems with particular structure, like factoring or simulating molecules.

cards.q: How many amplitudes does it take to fully describe the state of 50 qubits?
cards.why: 2⁵⁰, about 10¹⁵. The state of n qubits needs 2ⁿ amplitudes. That exponential growth is why ordinary computers struggle to simulate even modest quantum machines.

cards.title: Richard Feynman proposed quantum computers in 1981 to simulate nature — not to break codes.
cards.detail: He argued that nature is quantum mechanical, so simulating it efficiently needs a quantum machine. The code-breaking angle arrived in 1994 with Peter Shor's factoring algorithm.

cards.statement: Entangled qubits can be used to send messages faster than light.
cards.why: False. Entangled qubits give correlated results, but each side's outcomes alone look random. No usable information moves until the results are compared over an ordinary channel.

cards.title: Making a qubit in the real world

steps.p: Superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms and photons are all serious ways to build qubits, each backed by major companies and labs.
Superconducting qubits sit in refrigerators at around 10 to 20 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, to silence heat and noise.
Any stray interaction with the surroundings scrambles a qubit's state. Depending on the design, qubits hold it for microseconds up to seconds.

cards.aside: Every qubit design trades speed, quality and how easily it scales up.

cards.q: Roughly how cold are superconducting quantum chips kept?
options: About 0.01 K — colder than deep space
cards.why: Around 10–20 millikelvin. Deep space sits near 2.7 K. That extreme cold keeps the circuits superconducting and quiets the thermal noise that destroys quantum states.

options: A qubit losing its quantum state through contact with its surroundings
cards.why: Quantum information leaking away. Heat, vibration and stray fields disturb the fragile superposition. A computation must finish, or be error-corrected, before decoherence wins.

cards.statement: Trapped-ion quantum computers use individual charged atoms held in place by electric fields.
cards.why: True. Ions are trapped by electric fields and controlled with lasers. Every ion of an element is identical, giving very uniform qubits, though their operations run slower than superconducting ones.

cards.title: In 2019, Google said its Sycamore chip did in 200 seconds what a supercomputer would need 10,000 years for.
cards.detail: IBM disputed the estimate, arguing it would take days, and later classical methods narrowed the gap further. The task was a benchmark with no practical use.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT one of the leading ways to build qubits today?
cards.why: Vacuum tubes. They powered 1940s classical computers. Today's qubit contenders are superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons and electron spins in silicon.

cards.title: Where the speedups are

steps.p: Shor's algorithm factors large numbers dramatically faster than any known classical method, threatening RSA and other widely used public-key encryption.
Grover's algorithm searches unstructured data in about √N steps instead of N — a quadratic speedup, not an exponential one.
Chemistry and materials are quantum systems, so quantum computers may model them directly — the use Feynman originally imagined.

cards.aside: Everyday software like email, spreadsheets or video gains nothing from a quantum computer.

cards.q: With Grover's algorithm, roughly how many steps does it take to search 1,000,000 unsorted items?
cards.why: About 1,000. Grover needs roughly √N queries, and √1,000,000 is 1,000. In practice, error-correction overheads eat much of that gain.

cards.statement: A powerful quantum computer would make all encryption useless.
cards.why: False. Shor's algorithm threatens public-key schemes like RSA. Symmetric encryption such as AES mainly needs longer keys, and quantum-resistant public-key methods already exist.

cards.title: In 2024, the US standards body NIST published its first encryption standards designed to resist quantum computers.
cards.detail: They include ML-KEM for exchanging keys and ML-DSA for digital signatures, built on lattice math believed to withstand quantum attacks. Organizations are migrating now.

cards.q: What does "harvest now, decrypt later" refer to?
options: Attackers storing encrypted data today to decrypt once quantum computers are strong enough
Farming robots that use quantum sensors
Backing up data to quantum memory
cards.why: Store now, crack later. Secrets that must stay private for decades are already at risk, which is why governments push post-quantum migration years before a capable machine exists.

cards.statement: Grover's search algorithm gives an exponential speedup over classical search.
cards.why: False. It's quadratic: about √N steps instead of N. Useful, but far smaller than Shor's advantage for factoring, and often erased by real-world overheads.

lessons.title: Errors, hype and the road ahead

cards.title: Why error correction is the whole game

steps.p: Even the best operations still fail roughly once every few hundred to few thousand tries — far too often for long algorithms.
Error-correcting codes encode one reliable logical qubit in many physical qubits, and continually catch errors without disturbing the stored data.
Below a certain physical error rate, adding more qubits makes the logical qubit better rather than worse. Google demonstrated this with its Willow chip in 2024.

cards.aside: Useful machines will likely need thousands of logical qubits, each built from many physical ones.

cards.q: By recent estimates, roughly how many physical qubits might it take to break 2048-bit RSA encryption?
cards.why: Around a million. A 2025 Google estimate put it under a million noisy qubits running for about a week. Today's machines are far smaller and noisier.

cards.statement: A quantum computer with more qubits is always more powerful than one with fewer.
cards.why: False. Quality matters as much as quantity: error rates, connectivity and how long qubits stay coherent. A few hundred excellent qubits can beat thousands of noisy ones.

cards.title: Several "beyond any supercomputer" quantum results were later matched or approached by cleverer classical methods.
cards.detail: Better simulation techniques keep raising the bar, so claims of quantum advantage are now judged on whether the task is useful and whether classical experts have tried to beat it.

cards.q: What does NISQ, the name for today's era of quantum computing, stand for?
cards.why: Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum. Physicist John Preskill coined it in 2018 for machines with tens to thousands of imperfect qubits and no full error correction.

cards.title: Run quantum headlines through three questions
cards.body: Is the task actually useful? Are the qubits error-corrected? Has anyone tried hard to beat it on a classical computer? Most "breakthroughs" fail at least one.
cards.challenge: Find one quantum computing headline from this month and check it against those three questions.
